sections.h2: Your options for selling a house in Lansing
sections.html:
A Lansing owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or take a cash offer for the house as-is. Lansing is a Cook County village on the Indiana line, so a sale involves three layers of paperwork: the village for its seller certificate, the Cook County Clerk for recording and county transfer tax, and the State of Illinois for the transfer declaration.

Lansing is a home rule community, which gives the village more room than most to write its own local rules. That is why the village's own requirements get most of the space below.

Lansing sits 6.9 miles south of the Chicago city limits at 138th Street and about 25.6 miles from the Loop. Its neighbors are South Holland and Calumet City to the north, Thornton and Glenwood to the west, Lynwood to the south, and Munster and Hammond in Indiana to the east. The 2020 census counted 29,076 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 28,068.

The first settler family arrived in 1843 and the village incorporated in 1893. Buyers often like an established village, so a seller can mention that long local history.

Transportation options include Pace bus service, the Grand Trunk Western Main Line between Chicago and Port Huron, and the South Shore Line station at Munster Ridge in Indiana, which opened to riders on March 31, 2026. Most commuters still drive.

Housing here is affordable, and a median owner-occupied value of $177,000 is a useful anchor when you price. Figures below are 2020 to 2024 estimates.

The median monthly cost for owners without a mortgage is $825, so households that have paid off the house carry modest bills. Those owners sometimes consider a quick as-is sale after an inheritance or a move.

Two elementary districts and one high school district serve the village. District 158 runs Coolidge, Lester Crawl, Oak Glen and Reavis schools plus Memorial Junior High for grades 6 to 8. Sunnybrook District 171 runs Nathan Hale for PreK through grade 4 and Heritage Middle School for grades 5 to 8. Thornton Fractional South High School in District 215 takes students for grades 9 to 12.

Private and parochial options include St. Ann, Lansing Christian, Trinity Lutheran, Saint John Lutheran and Eagle Christian Academy. Buyers with children usually start by asking which of the two elementary districts covers a given address, so have the answer ready.

sections.h2: What Lansing requires when a house changes hands
sections.html:
The village, not the county, attaches its own condition to the sale. Lansing's rule, enacted May 21, 2013, makes the seller liable, and a certificate of payment from the village must be attached to the recording. There is no fee exemption.

  • Call the Lansing Municipal Center at 3141 Ridge Road, 708-895-7200, to learn how to obtain the certificate before the closing date.
  • Confirm the final stamp amount with the village before closing.
  • The state tax is 50 cents per $500 and the county tax is 25 cents per $500, with the seller named as the liable party for both.

Build the certificate into your closing timeline. A missing certificate can hold up the buyer's possession.

Residential water service needs a deposit of $100, paid at the Municipal Center after possession, with a driver's license and the closing documents. If a property has sat vacant four months or longer, the Building Commissioner must inspect it before that deposit is taken.

That last rule matters if you are selling a vacant or inherited house. Expect the buyer to need an inspection before water can be turned on, and consider scheduling it yourself so the sale is not held up.

  • Permits: the Building Department handles permits, contractor licenses and property maintenance, at (708) 895-7193. Four property maintenance inspectors investigate complaints and issue violation notices.
  • Vehicle stickers: new residents have 30 days to buy village stickers, and you must bring a closing document or lease.
  • Trash: each single-family home gets three toters, and yard waste collection runs April 1 through November 30.

A few small items fit in a folder you can hand over at closing. Vehicle stickers go on sale May 1 each year and expire June 30, and a buyer who moves in mid-year has 30 days to buy one. Dog and cat tags are required annually and go on sale in mid-May at the Municipal Center.

Garbage and recycling use village-issued toters that stay with the house, and leaves go in the green-lidded toter or brown paper bags from April 1 through November 30. Tree trimming is the property owner's job. For utilities, buyers call ComEd for electricity and Nicor Gas for gas. Leaving the toters, the service numbers and any pet or sticker records for the buyer shortens the first week after closing.

sections.h2: Does flooding affect selling a house in Lansing?
sections.html:
It can. The village keeps a flood information section covering the Little Calumet River, flood hazard, flood proofing and protection regulations, and it links to resources for Cook County residents affected by the storms and flooding of August 16 to 19, 2025. If your lot is near the river or has a history of basement water, gather any repair receipts and elevation or insurance paperwork before you list.

FEMA publishes the official flood maps at its Map Service Center, and the village can point you to its own guidance. A buyer's insurance quote often decides whether a deal closes, so being open about past water problems protects the sale.

sections.h2: When is a cash offer a reasonable choice in Lansing?
sections.html:
With a median owner-occupied value of $177,000, a large repair bill takes a bigger share of the price. If the roof, sewer line or basement needs work and you would rather not manage contractors, a cash buyer who takes the house as-is removes that step. Ask for a closing date in writing, ask who pays for the seller certificate, and confirm the buyer's title company will submit the transfer declaration.

A cash sale also skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, so the village certificate is usually the item to schedule first. Keep a copy of the certificate and your closing documents, since you will need them again if a title question comes up later.

faqs.q: Who pays transfer tax when selling in Lansing?
faqs.a: The seller is liable for the state tax, the Cook County tax and Lansing's own certificate of payment. Confirm final amounts with the village before closing.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection before the buyer gets water?
faqs.a: Only if the property has been vacant four months or more. In that case the Building Commissioner must inspect before the $100 water deposit is accepted. An occupied house goes straight to deposit and application at the Municipal Center.

faqs.q: Which office handles permits in Lansing?
faqs.a: The Building Department at the Lansing Municipal Center handles permits and contractor licenses. Call (708) 895-7193 before starting any home improvement. Most improvements need a permit.
Thornton Fractional South High School, part of District 215, serves the village. Elementary students attend either District 158 or Sunnybrook District 171 depending on the address.

faqs.q: Is Lansing in a flood-prone area?
faqs.a: Parts of the area sit near the Little Calumet River, and the village publishes flood hazard and protection information. Check the FEMA flood map for your parcel and ask your insurer before listing.
